title: Valuation Ratios and the Long-Run Stock Market Outlook
research_question: Do valuation ratios such as the price-dividend and price-earnings ratios contain information about future real stock price growth, and does this informational content differ between short and long forecast horizons? Furthermore, can the apparent stronger relationship at long horizons be explained by the statistical properties of finite samples or by nonlinearities in how stock prices adjust toward fundamentals?
data_description: The study uses annual U.S. stock market data spanning 1872–1997, drawn from Campbell and Shiller (1998) and originally based on the S&P 500 index. Key variables include the nominal stock price index, nominal dividends, and nominal earnings, each deflated by the consumer price index to obtain real stock prices, real dividends, and real earnings. From these, two valuation ratios are constructed in log-levels: the price-dividend ratio (January real stock price divided by real dividends over the previous calendar year) and the price-earnings ratio (January real stock price divided by real earnings over the previous calendar year). The unit of observation is the aggregate U.S. stock market at annual frequency. Forecast horizons examined range from 1 to 10 years for real stock price growth.
institutional_context: The setting is the long-run behavior of the aggregate U.S. equity market, where measures of fundamental value such as dividends and earnings are widely believed to anchor stock prices over extended horizons. A recurring empirical pattern in financial economics is that valuation ratios appear weakly related to short-term price movements but strongly related to multi-year price changes, a finding highlighted in classic work by Fama and French and by Campbell and Shiller. This pattern has motivated debate about whether stock prices revert to fundamentals slowly, whether arbitrage is limited by the risks of betting against persistent mispricing by noise traders, and whether the adjustment toward equilibrium is faster when valuations deviate substantially from fundamentals. The 1872–1997 sample spans multiple market regimes, including episodes of pronounced over- and undervaluation, providing a rich setting for examining mean-reversion in valuation ratios.
